sample.Description_1: Bay View State Park is a 66-acre camping park with 1,285-feet of saltwater shoreline. The park offers views of the San Juan Islands fronting Padilla Bay, one of 15 existing national marine estuaries.
sample.Fieldwork_Observations:
•	The south shore is threatened by bluff erosion adjacent to Edison Road/Bayview Road.

•	The park was built on fill on intertidal spawning habitat which both prevents sediment movement and reduces intertidal spawning habitats.

sample.Description_1: Belfair State Park is a 94-acre, year-round camping park on 3,720 feet of saltwater shoreline at the southern end of Hood Canal in western Washington. It is noted for its saltwater tide flats and wetlands.
sample.Fieldwork_Observations:
• The lower camp loop septic tank becomes inundated with saltwater at high tide.

• The campground floods in the winter and many full-service sites are impacted. Overland flooding originates from the road, not coastal flooding, in the winter.

sample.Description_1: Birch Bay State Park is a 664-acre camping park with 8,255 feet of saltwater shoreline on Birch Bay and 14,923 feet of freshwater shoreline on Terrell Creek. The park is rich in shellfish resources.
sample.Fieldwork_Observations:
•	Birch Bay Drive parallels the shoreline, chronically floods, and is shut down during King Tides and high-water events. Large erosional scour holes have formed beneath the waterward shoulder. The road is owned by Whatcom County and has many utilities underneath and alongside the road, including: water, sewer, and fiber optic cable that serve the park and the Birch Bay community to the south.

•	During king tides and storm surges, water in Terrell Creek rises within one foot of the bottom of the Helwig Road vehicle bridge. The pedestrian bridges over the creek have low freeboard and utilities running underneath. Logs catch during high water events.

•	The CXT toilet near the boat launch is located in a wetland and surrounded by water on three sides from Terrell Creek. The toilet regularly floods during high water events and must be pumped out at the end of summer.
